papers.title: Kameleo: In-Situ Activation-Precision Selection for Bit-Serial LLM Accelerators
papers.headline: Choose activation precision from deployment data
papers.authors: Robin Geens, Thomas Debelle, Marian Verhelst, Chao Fang
papers.summary: Kameleo replaces offline precision calibration with local output comparisons.
papers.problem: Bit-serial accelerators process activation mantissa bits sequentially; shorter mantissas save cycles. Prior calibration repeatedly evaluates whole-model perplexity, a next-token prediction uncertainty measure. Settings selected on one dataset can lose quality on another.

method.title: Reuse partial sums
method.description: Kameleo captures reduced-precision candidates during full-precision computation: intermediate sums already contain the shorter-mantissa results. Extra registers preserve candidates for comparison.

method.title: Select, then lock
method.description: A local rule counts outputs exceeding a relative-error tolerance. Two passes narrow nine candidate lengths, then lock each GEMM’s precision. Selection uses deployment tokens; outputs remain usable. Reselection timing is an operating policy. The shortest passing length wins; fewer retained bits shorten subsequent computation.

results.finding: 2.12–2.29× fewer prefill matrix-unit cycles on WikiText2
results.setup: Four models, INT4 weights; cycle baseline: FP16 activations. Perplexity degradation stayed below 1% against full 11-bit block-floating activations, which share exponents across groups.

papers.limitations: Software precision emulation and RTL cycle simulation, not silicon measurements; no independent reproduction here. A local error proxy cannot guarantee future task accuracy.
papers.implications: AI interpretation — systems/chips: For an NPU supplier, the product opportunity is reducing customer-specific calibration work. The adoption test should pair a drifting customer workload with task acceptance checks and a defined fallback precision. Runtime owners must decide when to reselect and account for the slower selection period. Measure end-to-end latency and energy through those transitions before committing hardware area: matrix-unit cycle savings alone cannot establish cost per successful task.

papers.title: Accelerating Mixture of Block Attention via Dynamic Routing, KV-Centric Execution and Runtime Pipelining
papers.headline: Make sparse attention reuse the data it selects
papers.authors: Yingqi Shi, Junru Lu, Yun Liu, Di Yin, Xing Sun
papers.summary: LightningMoBA combines adaptive block selection with GPU work scheduling. The useful change is turning an irregular sparse pattern into work that reuses KV data and overlaps transfers with computation.
papers.problem: Mixture of Block Attention (MoBA) scores groups of keys and keeps selected blocks for each query. FlashMoBA uses a fixed Top-k count and assigns work by query range. That can retain weak blocks for one query while dropping useful ones for another. Separate query ranges can also reload the same KV block, leaving fewer useful rows per matrix tile. Reduced attention arithmetic therefore need not translate into proportional speedup.

method.title: Select by relative score, rather than a fixed count
method.description: LightningMoBA keeps optional blocks whose scores lie within a margin of that query’s strongest preceding block. A sharply concentrated query can retain fewer blocks; a diffuse query can retain more. Required initial and nearby blocks remain. The scorer and model weights stay unchanged. Held-out calibration sets the threshold to match an average retention budget, rather than enforcing that count on every query.

method.title: Group consumers around the KV block
method.description: Within each query head, selected query rows are grouped by the KV block they need. Each work unit reuses its loaded K/V tile across those rows. Fanout—the number of queries selecting a block—can be highly uneven. Popular blocks are therefore divided into bounded tasks, trading some repeated loads for better parallelism and a shorter scheduling tail.

method.title: Overlap two different access patterns
method.description: On Hopper, contiguous K/V transfers and irregular query gathers use separate producer paths while Tensor Cores compute. The released default kernel requires SM90, CUDA 12.3 or later, BF16 inputs and head dimension 128. Its sparse prefill is paired with dense decoding in the main evaluation.

results.finding: Table 1 reports 1.20–1.60× generation-loop speedups across five checkpoints.
results.setup: Author measurements versus FlashMoBA: 6,500 RULER examples, 4K–128K contexts, batch 1, tensor parallelism 8, matched average Top-16 retention; both use CUDA Graph dense decode. RULER tests long-context retrieval and reasoning.

papers.limitations: Not independently reproduced. Table 1 and the repository agree on the speedup range above; adjacent paper prose gives a different range. Quality gains are uneven, including regressions at some lengths. The timing covers an evaluation loop, not a production latency guarantee. Hopper-specific pipelining and batch-one tests limit direct extrapolation.
papers.implications: AI interpretation: For a long-document service, test accepted answers per GPU-hour at the required tail latency, including failures caused by omitted context. Assign threshold calibration and regression checks to the serving team. For an NPU designer, investigate concurrent indexed gathers, regular transfers and matrix work before projecting these gains onto different hardware; sparse FLOP counts alone miss that execution requirement.

papers.title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
papers.headline: Make quantization search cheap enough to repeat for each model
papers.authors: Xingyang Li, Tianlang Zhao, Song Han, Ligeng Zhu · MIT and NVIDIA
papers.summary: QDA combines an agent, reusable quantizers, and a fast evaluator to search for model-specific recipes that retain existing serving formats.
papers.problem: Quantization recipes combine transformations, rounding, scales, and calibration data. Their ranking changes with model and precision. Layer-local error misses accumulated effects, while repeatedly generating long reasoning answers makes full evaluation expensive. Combining separate research implementations also consumes engineering time.

method.title: Build many compatible candidates
method.description: The agent proposes a recipe, builds it, reads feedback, and chooses the next change. The authors describe 21 composable post-training quantization methods and searches trying up to 36 candidates in eight hours. A shared library makes combinations practical without reimplementing every method during each search. Checkpoints must preserve the baseline format and use existing kernels.

method.title: Compare the served model’s predictions
method.description: KL divergence measures how two probability distributions differ. QDA compares candidate next-token probabilities with the original model on hidden reference traces, using the actual serving kernel. Cached teacher probabilities make scoring cheap; the evaluator retains the top 128 tokens and groups the remainder. Thus the score captures errors that appear only in serving, while the agent cannot calibrate directly on the hidden traces.

method.title: Check whether reasoning actually finishes
method.description: Promising candidates also generate complete answers. This exposes repetition and truncation that scoring fixed prefixes can miss. The agent uses both signals to revise the recipe; only its final submission receives benchmark evaluation. The diagram separates routine scoring from these selective checks.

results.finding: Higher accuracy at fixed quantization formats
results.setup: Author-reported four-model study on GH200 with vLLM: average gains of 0.9/1.4/2.2 percentage points over the strongest public recipe at W4A16/W4A8/W3A16; 64 GPU-hours per search.

papers.limitations: Preprint; not independently reproduced here. KL is a proxy, and limited generation checks cannot establish reliability across customer workloads. Final benchmark evaluation is outside the search budget.
papers.implications:
AI interpretation — For a model-serving team, the decision is whether repeated recipe search releases a useful checkpoint sooner than manual tuning. Compare total search, final validation, and engineer effort against the resulting task quality at your required precision. Keep production latency and cost per accepted task in that comparison.

For an accelerator team, test the evaluator on the exact kernel, scale format, and workload intended for deployment. A recipe that fits a supported format can reduce adoption work, but that does not establish portability to another runtime. Assign an owner to the quantizer–kernel contract and retain customer-specific acceptance tests.

papers.title: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration
papers.headline: Spend simulator calls on designs that can remove the bottleneck
papers.authors: Yicheng He, Yuqi Xue, Tianyang Wu, Jian Huang, Bin Hu · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
papers.venue: arXiv · cs.AR · v1; authors report NeurIPS 2026 acceptance
papers.summary: CriticNPU uses a calibrated hardware model to screen proposed NPU designs before simulation and guide subsequent changes.
papers.problem: Scalar latency ranks designs but poorly explains which resource to change. Black-box search spends evaluations learning that relationship; diagnosis alone cannot screen the next candidate.

method.title: Separate proposal from evaluation
method.description: The released implementation uses LLM agents for workload extraction and architecture proposals, deterministic calculations for the critic, and NeuSIM for latency, power, and memory evaluation. Prefill and decode designs are optimized separately.

method.title: Calibrate the bottleneck model
method.description: Roofline bounds throughput by compute capacity and bandwidth times arithmetic intensity. CriticNPU learns attainable fractions of those ceilings per operator type from simulation feedback, correcting classifications based on overstated peak resources.

method.title: Filter, then feed evidence back
method.description: After warm-up, the critic skips candidates predicted worse than the incumbent. For simulated designs, it summarizes phase-specific bottlenecks and estimates small parameter changes, directing the planner toward the limiting resource.

results.finding: Near-best designs with fewer evaluations
results.setup: Author-reported NeuSIM study: six LLMs × 16 settings; approximately 54 calls versus 2.2–2.4× as many for classical baselines. Best-or-tied latency: 74% prefill, 87.5% decode.

papers.limitations: Simulation, not silicon measurement; not independently reproduced here. Irregular MoE behavior weakens the model: DeepSeek-V3 decode wins were 8/16 versus Bayesian optimization’s 15/16.
papers.implications:
AI interpretation — The customer is an architecture team with a queue of expensive evaluations. Pilot the critic against your current search at equal simulation budgets, then compare the best feasible design reached, total elapsed time, and engineering review. Fewer calls become useful only if the filter preserves candidates that matter for the product.

Audit a sample of rejected proposals with the full simulator. Track missed improvements separately from prediction error: a useful average estimate can still reject the winning design. Assign ownership of operator profiles and calibration to the performance-modeling team, with architecture engineers approving resource trade-offs. For an irregular MoE target, retain a broader search path until the critic demonstrates reliable screening on representative routing and load. Search efficiency alone cannot establish lower manufacturing cost or better customer task economics.

papers.title: Multi-Branch Transformer
papers.headline: Parallel block paths share memory, but need an engine that uses it
papers.authors: Gaotang Li, Lingjie Chen, Chunyuan Deng, Zhiwei Xu, Hongzheng Chen, Christopher De Sa, Jingrui He, Yingheng Wang, Hanghang Tong
papers.summary: MBT reorganizes a Transformer’s middle layers into parallel branches, then shares KV across branches at each depth. Architecture and serving changes address separate costs.
papers.problem: A serial stack makes each block wait for its predecessor. Branching exposes concurrent work, but private branch caches multiply stored state. Even shared caches can be reread separately, so changing the model graph alone does not guarantee faster execution.

method.title: Split full blocks, then fuse
method.description: Every token traverses shared initial blocks, all independently parameterized branches, and shared final blocks. Fusion normalizes branch outputs, concatenates them, and projects back to the shared width. The Balanced variant adjusts branch width and depth together at comparable training compute.

method.title: Build common memory at each depth
method.description: Joint-KV concatenates normalized branch inputs and projects them into shared keys and values. Queries, residual streams, and MoE computations remain branch-specific. Sharing occurs across branches at the same depth, requiring coordination there. Joint-KV is trained, so existing models require architectural adaptation.

method.title: Execute branches together; reuse reads
method.description: Branch grouping batches same-depth blocks into one execution stage. Head folding combines branch query heads into one grouped-query attention call, reducing repeated reads of shared KV. Each query head retains its own softmax. The engine preserves the trained computation while changing its execution schedule.

results.finding: 1.12–1.50× decode throughput, averaged over four model scales.
results.setup: Four-branch Balanced Joint-KV versus same-scale Standard; one H200, BF16-trained checkpoints, 4K–128K inputs, 1K outputs, temperature 1.0, tested concurrency 1–64. Excludes prefill.

results.finding: All 12 final models had lower validation loss than Standard.
results.setup: Two, three, or four branches across 0.8B–2.1B MoE scales, comparable training compute; 4,096-token training context.

papers.limitations: Long-context runs measure speed, not usable long-context quality: generation exceeds the training window. Author-reported results, not independently reproduced. The public code emphasizes pretraining; inference measurements use a dedicated implementation.
papers.implications: AI interpretation — systems and product decisions: A model team should evaluate branch allocation and serving support together. For a long-document product, verify retrieval and answer quality at the intended context before translating reduced KV traffic into a capacity plan. A runtime team should price the custom execution work and ongoing maintenance against accepted tasks per device at the required latency. A chip team should test the resulting attention shapes and synchronization costs before treating architectural parallelism as a hardware advantage.

papers.title: LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
papers.headline: Fill the loop pipeline without another trained drafter
papers.authors: Siqi Zhu, Suozhi Huang, Yi Zhao, Jiaxuan You
papers.summary: LoopFill combines retrieved continuations and early predictions to start future tokens sooner.
papers.problem: Looped Transformers reuse layers repeatedly per token. Earlier pipelines start the next token from a shallow-loop prediction, but still wait for that drafting depth, leaving gaps.

method.title: Retrieve, then extend
method.description: A suffix tree indexes previous text. Matching endings retrieves continuations without model computation. LoopFill merges these with shallow-loop predictions in one candidate tree; either source can extend the other.

method.title: Budget, verify, reuse
method.description: Path scores combine retrieval frequencies and model probabilities. Top candidates advance together through the shared block at different depths. Full-depth verification determines emitted tokens; accepted branches retain completed work. No additional training is required.

results.finding: 5.85× decode speedup over autoregressive decoding; LoopAhead achieved 4.19×.
results.setup: Ouro-2.6B, seven-benchmark mean, greedy, one request; single NVIDIA L20X, BF16. Decode timing excludes prefill.

results.finding: 1.6% throughput gain over LoopAhead.
results.setup: Same model/hardware, SpecBench, temperature 1.0, concurrency 16; includes prefill.

papers.limitations: Unpredictable continuations weaken retrieval. Extra drafts compete with concurrent requests. Author measurements; not independently reproduced.
papers.implications: AI interpretation — systems and product decisions: For a team considering a looped model, evaluate the scheduler together with model quality before choosing hardware or committing to a response-time target. Test the actual request mix at both light load and peak concurrency. Count prefill, suffix lookup, rejected computation, and memory consumed by drafts in the cost per accepted task. A latency improvement at light load may justify an interactive product, while the same drafting budget may be inappropriate for a busy shared service. Assign runtime ownership for tuning that budget as traffic changes.

papers.title: MMFlash: Faster Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models
papers.headline: Train the drafter on the image-dependent tokens that cut verification short
papers.authors: Sicheng Feng, Zigeng Chen, Song Wang, Gongfan Fang, Xinchao Wang
papers.summary: MMFlash trains a speculative drafter to better predict text that depends on visual evidence. It also reduces the context the drafter attends to on long video prompts.
papers.problem: DFlash fills a block of masked token positions in one pass using features from the target model. The target checks the proposals in parallel and accepts a contiguous prefix. One early miss can discard otherwise usable work. DFlash weights training errors by position. In the authors’ diagnostic, tokens most dependent on the image were accepted less often, even after training the baseline on multimodal data.

method.title: Measure what the image changes
method.description: Offline, hold the text prefix fixed and run the target with and without the image. Compare its next-token probabilities using KL divergence, a measure of how much one probability distribution differs from another. Give the strongest training signal to changes on which the image-conditioned target is confident.

method.title: Spend training effort where it can extend the accepted prefix
method.description: The loss favors positions likely to survive verification, estimated from drafter confidence across the prefix. A visual bonus is larger when the drafter gives the target token low probability and fades as that prediction improves. For example, learning the digit read from a chart can preserve the rest of the draft if that digit would otherwise be the first rejection.

method.title: Thin the draft context for long video
method.description: The drafter reads target features and skips most distant visual positions, retaining regularly spaced visual tokens, all text, a recent window and a few initial tokens. The paper uses this sparse pattern during training and serving. The target still verifies the proposed text.

results.finding: About 3× average decode speed versus ordinary autoregressive decoding and 10–11% over DFlash.
results.setup: Seven image benchmarks, Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, greedy decoding, concurrency one, SGLang on one H200. Author measurements.

papers.limitations: The paper measures decode speed. Gains over ordinary decoding generally shrink with concurrency, and long video remains harder to draft than images. Independent reproduction was not verified.
papers.implications: AI interpretation — For an interactive document assistant, pilot the paired draft and target checkpoints where users wait for a long answer after uploading an image. Measure end-to-end latency and GPU cost per accepted answer at the traffic mix you actually serve. If image encoding or prefill dominates the wait, or the drafter consumes memory needed for batching, the decode gain may do little for users or fleet cost. Include the cost of qualifying a new drafter when the target model changes.

papers.title: Factored One-sided Adam-Moment for Practical and Scalable SOAP
papers.headline: FOAM cuts the cost of SOAP by rotating gradients along one axis
papers.authors: Jaemyung Yu, Byeongho Heo, Sangdoo Yun, Dongyoon Han · NAVER AI Lab
papers.summary: FOAM is a training optimizer that keeps SOAP’s input-side gradient rotation and compresses its running variance estimate.
papers.problem: AdamW scales each gradient coordinate using its own history. SOAP first rotates gradients into a basis derived from input and output gradient correlations, then applies Adam-style scaling there. This is preconditioning: changing the directions and sizes of updates to account for how the loss responds to movement. SOAP stores a square factor and a basis for each axis, periodically recomputes both bases, and retains a full matrix of squared-gradient averages. For a training team, fewer steps only pay off if these extra operations and buffers leave a net gain in time or usable memory.

method.title: Keep the input rotation
method.description: For a weight matrix with m outputs and n inputs, FOAM keeps the n-by-n input factor and removes the m-by-m output factor and its eigendecomposition. The authors motivate the choice with evidence that the output-side curvature is often close to diagonal. If it is diagonal, output channels can have different scales without mixing their directions.

method.title: Reconstruct the squared-gradient averages from two vectors
method.description: FOAM tracks running row and column means of squared gradients after rotation. Their outer product, normalized to match the input factor’s trace, estimates the second moment with m+n stored numbers instead of mn. Under the paper’s separable covariance assumption, the rotated variance factors into one term per output and one per input direction. The first-moment buffer stays dense.

results.finding: 10.53 hours for FOAM versus 22.66 hours for SOAP to reach AdamW’s final validation loss of 2.847.
results.setup: Authors’ GPT-2-scale 760M FineWeb run on eight H100s, BF16 mixed precision, tuned optimizers and 0.5M tokens per batch. At the full step budget, validation loss was 2.796 for FOAM and 2.791 for SOAP.

papers.limitations: The main comparisons reach 760M parameters. Wide input layers still carry a quadratic factor, and strong correlations across output channels can weaken the approximation. These are author measurements without independent reproduction. The authors’ repository says implementation release is pending.
papers.implications: AI interpretation. If a training team uses SOAP for convergence but is running out of accelerator memory or losing time to basis refreshes, FOAM is a candidate for the next controlled run. Compare GPU-hours to the team’s own validation target and measure peak allocated memory under its actual sharding scheme. If the gain comes from lower optimizer state, check whether it frees enough headroom for a larger batch or fewer shards. The paper’s fixed-loss time comparison does not price either change.

papers.title: SoScale: Second-Order Scale Search for FP4 Quantization
papers.headline: Choosing FP4 scales by the errors a layer actually sees
papers.authors: Pengxiang Zhao, Xing Li, Hui-Ling Zhen, Weizhe Lin, Xianzhi Yu, Zhenhua Dong · Huawei Technologies
papers.summary: SoScale uses layer output error to select FP4 weight scales during calibration.
papers.problem: A block scale determines which real values the fixed FP4 payload can represent. Scaling to the largest magnitude gives outliers room but spreads the grid across a wider range, leaving smaller weights with coarser steps. ScaleSearch tries nearby representable scales and picks the one with the smallest squared rounding error across weights. That improves the fit to the weight block. In a linear projection, though, the same rounding error can have different effects depending on which input channel carries it and which other channels are active.

method.title: Score each legal scale by its effect on the projection
method.description: For each block, SoScale rounds weights under nearby hardware-valid scale codes and scores the resulting error vector with a submatrix of XᵀX, where X contains calibration inputs. This matrix is proportional to the Hessian, the curvature of the layer's squared output-error objective. Its diagonal captures channel energy and its off-diagonal entries capture how channels vary together. For example, errors of opposite sign can cancel when their inputs move together. A weight-only squared error score would count both errors separately.

method.title: Let later blocks absorb earlier rounding errors
method.description: GPTQ uses inverse-Hessian information to adjust unquantized weights after rounding. SoScale applies this at the FP4 block boundary. It commits a block, uses a factor of the damped inverse Hessian to distribute its residual into the remaining working weights, then searches the next scale on those adjusted values. This accounts for interactions across blocks without searching every combination of scale codes jointly. The weight search happens during calibration. Inference uses the resulting weights and scales in the original FP4 format.

results.finding: Mean benchmark score rose from 74.16% to 74.79% versus ScaleSearch.
results.setup: Authors’ Table 2, Qwen3-14B, MXFP4 W4A4 with per-token activation scaling, seven tasks, no Hadamard preprocessing for either method.

papers.limitations: Author-reported benchmark accuracy, without independent reproduction. The evaluation does not establish end-to-end latency, throughput or cost on native FP4 hardware.
papers.implications: AI interpretation. For an NPU team whose existing FP4 kernel passes latency targets but misses a customer's quality threshold, an offline scale search is worth testing before changing the arithmetic format. Compare matched checkpoints with the same activation path and kernel, then measure the share of real tasks accepted without a higher-precision retry. Include calibration and requalification effort for each checkpoint refresh. The decision depends on whether quality gains survive the actual input mix and make the FP4 path cheaper per accepted task.

papers.title: One-Sided Expert-Parallel All-to-All for Mixture-of-Experts Inference over NVLink
papers.headline: MoE decode can spend more time coordinating than transferring
papers.authors: Bo Li, Chulian Zhang, Or Biri, Anthony Chang, Anton Korzh, Noam Duvdevani, XingFei Xi, Daniel Stokes, Zhenhuan Chen, Ludwig Schneider, Artem Y. Polyakov, Julien Demouth, Chandler Zhou · NVIDIA
papers.summary: NVLinkOneSided cuts the fixed cost of routing tokens between experts on different GPUs. Its advantage is clearest when each decode step carries few tokens.
papers.problem: Expert parallelism distributes experts across GPUs. Each layer sends token activations to the selected experts and returns their outputs. At small batches, coordination and receive-side regrouping can take longer than transferring the payload.

method.title: Write once per destination GPU
method.description: The sender writes into its own reserved region of each peer’s buffer. It skips a preliminary routing exchange and sends one activation even when multiple experts on that peer need it.

method.title: Gather inputs by index
method.description: The receiver builds per-expert slot lists. Grouped matrix multiplies gather activations using those indices, avoiding a separate copy into expert order.

method.title: Match completion signaling to batch size
method.description: Fence compacts slots and signals completion per peer. Sentinel polls reserved bit patterns in each landing slot to detect arrival. This shortens the synchronization path for small batches, while copying and resetting slots costs more as batches grow.

results.finding: 17.4 μs versus 47.9 μs for dispatch plus combine
results.setup: Author measurements against DeepEP on eight B300 GPUs, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash layer shape, one token per GPU, MXFP8 dispatch and BF16 combine.

papers.limitations: The method requires one NVLink domain and reserves more buffer space as the expert group grows. Fused MegaMoE led at larger batches on eight B300s. Evidence comes from layer and communication benchmarks without independent reproduction.
papers.implications: AI interpretation — For a team serving interactive MoE traffic, benchmark this path before paying for more bandwidth. Replay real routing and batch sizes, then measure p99 time per output token and completed requests per GPU-hour at the same latency target. If the workload already spends most of the step on expert compute, faster collectives may barely move customer latency. A chip team should benchmark small-message completion and peer-buffer access alongside bulk link throughput before deciding which part of the interconnect to optimize.

papers.title: ForeSpark: Joint Draft and Verification Budget Scheduling for Parallel Speculative Decoding
papers.headline: ForeSpark cuts draft work before verification
papers.authors: Jaeyong Song, Daniel Wang, Pratyush Patel, Jonny Kong, Preyas Shah, Shobhit Kanaujia
papers.summary: ForeSpark decides how many tokens each request should draft before the GPU runs the drafter, then assigns verification across the batch.
papers.problem: A parallel drafter proposes several future tokens in one pass. The target model checks those proposals and accepts a prefix. DSpark can cut verification work by checking only promising prefixes, but it still generates the full drafts. Under load, discarded proposals take GPU time away from requests already sharing the batch.

method.title: Estimate the payoff before drafting
method.description: A small predictor reads the target model’s latest context features and token embedding. It estimates, for each candidate draft length, the chance that each prefix survives verification. Draft length can change earlier proposals because draft positions attend to one another.

method.title: Budget both passes together
method.description: The scheduler ranks marginal expected token gains across requests and uses profiled GPU timings to choose draft lengths and a batch-wide verification budget. It looks for the most expected accepted tokens per unit of step time. Packing variable-length drafts removes the unused positions from the drafter’s input.

method.title: Spend verification on the drafts that materialize
method.description: After drafting, a second predictor scores the actual prefixes. The target verifies the best-ranked prefixes within budget using standard speculative sampling, which preserves its output distribution.

results.finding: 20% higher sustainable request rate than the strongest baseline
results.setup: Author-measured vLLM replay of multi-turn ShareGPT traffic, Qwen3-14B in BF16 on eight H100s, versus ordinary autoregressive decoding. Capacity requires 90% of requests to meet both first-token and per-output-token latency targets.

papers.limitations: The benchmark was not independently reproduced. Global ranking can leave some requests without a draft on a given step.
papers.implications: AI interpretation — For an interactive serving team deciding whether to add replicas, first replay peak customer traffic with joint scheduling and measure the GPU-hours per request that meets both latency targets. Break out those results by request type. An aggregate capacity gain is worth less if a high-priority customer workflow still needs reserved capacity because its requests rarely get useful drafts.

papers.title: When Is High-Bandwidth Flash Cost-Effective for LLM Inference?
papers.headline: Can flash memory replace the GPUs bought for capacity?
papers.authors: Zhiyu An, Yiping Li, Wan Du · UC Merced
papers.summary: HBF adds storage near GPUs. This study asks when latency and cost justify it.
papers.problem: Models can outgrow GPU memory before exhausting compute. Host offloading adds movement delays, while replacing fast memory with flash can damage bandwidth.

method.title: Stream cold weights; keep active state close
method.description: Active attention state stays near the GPU; cold weights stream from flash. Mixture-of-experts models activate selected experts per token. Consequently, the relevant traffic is the weights each batch touches, not the total stored model size.

method.title: Compare adding memory with replacing it
method.description: Shared-site HBF sacrifices some near-memory capacity and bandwidth; cascaded HBF preserves them. The comparison tests whether added capacity compensates for weakening the fast working set. Those two integration choices should not be treated as equivalent.

method.title: Ask three separate questions: does it fit, respond fast enough, and cost less?
method.description:
The released evaluation compares nine models, five workloads, two GPU platforms and installations of 1–100 GPUs. It asks about the cheapest passing installation at fixed demand separately from useful throughput at a fixed GPU count. The authors provide simulator code, timing profiles, workload inputs and archived outputs; we have not independently reproduced them.

Illustration, not a paper result: replacing four extra GPUs with one flash tier saves money only if the tier costs less than those GPUs and still meets the response-time target. More capacity alone does not answer either question.

results.finding: 32 GPUs → 4 in one simulated example
results.setup: Qwen3-235B, RTX 4090-scale, four short-chat users; BF16, 512/64 input/output tokens. First-token/mean-token/p99-token limits: 5 s/100 ms/200 ms.

papers.limitations: Simulation, not hardware measurement. Just two of 14 audited GPU-count wins survive every sensitivity setting. Quantization or different serving policies may change the answer.
papers.implications: For a deployment buying extra GPUs mainly to fit weights, HBF is a possible memory-expansion product. The purchasing test is total installed cost at the required quality, load and latency, compared with quantization or additional GPUs. A chip team should validate that customer segment before optimizing peak bandwidth: the opportunity shrinks if a cheaper software change removes the capacity constraint. Component-level savings still need a full-system cost check.

papers.title: TriAttention: Unified Sparse Mixed-Precision Attention for Long-Context LLM Inference
papers.headline: Spend precision where attention needs it
papers.authors: Hanzhi Zhang, Qiao Zhang, Qinglei Cao, Heng Fan, Yan Huang, Kewei Sha, Yunhe Feng
papers.summary: A three-way attention policy combines skipping, INT4 and INT8, then preserves its savings in the cache used during generation. Offline calibration selects the policy before inference.
papers.problem: Long prompts create two costs: comparing token pairs during prompt processing, then rereading earlier keys and values for every generated token. Sparsity removes comparisons but can discard useful context. Uniform low precision keeps context cheaply but also reduces numerical accuracy in sensitive interactions. Treating retention and precision separately limits that trade-off.

method.title: Keep, approximate or skip
method.description: Each head gets two distance boundaries that divide attention tiles into INT8, INT4 and skipped regions. The intermediate option retains interactions that tolerate approximation but would be harmful to remove. A compact boundary table replaces a context-sized policy, while fused attention combines retained regions into one normalized output.

method.title: Allocate by measured damage, then check quality
method.description: The released calibration code compares candidate outputs after the attention output projection and normalizes their error, so heads can be compared on a common scale. Its allocator searches error-plus-cost choices across all heads; the cost includes both retained tile counts and their precision. Selection then evaluates complete model predictions, choosing the cheapest candidate that passes every represented length group. The code checks both prediction-distribution divergence and deterioration in reference-response likelihood. This second check matters because small errors in individual heads can accumulate across the model.

method.title: Carry the savings into each generated token
method.description: The decode implementation packs retained prompt blocks into INT4/INT8 buffers instead of preserving a full prompt cache. When several query heads share keys and values, it stores the union they need and uses the highest requested key precision, preventing one head's compression choice from removing another head's evidence. Per-head masks preserve their different access patterns. Newly generated keys and values go into a separate BF16 tail. The practical benefit is less prompt data to read repeatedly, rather than only a faster initial prompt pass.

results.finding: Complete-request throughput increased about 1.62×: 22.80 versus 14.06 tokens/s.
results.setup: Authors' Table 1: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, A100-SXM4 40GB, batch 1, 65,536 input and 128 output tokens; BF16 SDPA baseline.

results.finding: 64K LooGLE-SD quality remained close: 47.94 versus BF16's 48.40.
results.setup: Authors' LV-Eval experiment with the same Llama model; this is one task, not a guarantee for every workload.

papers.limitations: Calibration and candidate selection require representative samples and additional offline work. The repository targets particular model configurations and NVIDIA CUDA hardware. Editorial caution: passing those sample-based quality checks does not establish reliability on a different domain, model or context distribution; the reported performance was not independently reproduced here.
papers.implications: For a document-analysis service, the opportunity is to process long customer inputs at lower cost while preserving the answers that matter. Before adopting the kernel, compare cost per acceptable response on representative documents, including calibration, integration and regression-testing effort. The commercial benefit depends on end-to-end savings surviving that quality threshold; attention speed alone does not establish a cheaper service.

papers.headline: Schedule the return trip from tools to GPUs
papers.authors: Shuhuai Li, Shengdong Ye, Dongdong Ge, Yinyu Ye, Jianghao Lin
papers.summary: An agent alternates between generating text and waiting for tools. TAO coordinates which sessions return to which GPU servers, using cache value, tool readiness and capacity together.
papers.problem: Load balancing can spread requests evenly or favor a server with reusable context. Neither alone says when a tool will finish. Choosing sessions one by one can also fill capacity before a better combination is considered.

method.title: Release the execution slot while a tool runs
method.description:
When a session calls an external tool, TAO moves it to a shared waiting pool, freeing GPU execution capacity for other sessions. The tool continues on the CPU side. Execution capacity is distinct from physical context storage: the inference engine still manages the attention cache and its eviction.

Illustration: a coding assistant waiting for a test should not prevent another ready assistant from using an available execution slot.

method.title: Compare cache value, readiness and size in order
method.description:
For each session–server pair, TAO first considers cache reuse value discounted over time, then near-term tool-return readiness, then token footprint. These priorities are ordered rather than mixed into a hand-tuned weighted score. Runtime hints and past tool durations help predict readiness.

The useful distinction is between having reusable work and being ready to use it. A fast return to the wrong server can still require repeated computation.

method.title: Choose a feasible group, not just the next session
method.description:
An asynchronous dynamic program compares groups of sessions and their placements within server capacity. Before applying a plan, it rechecks current capacity and session state.

Think of packing several boxes together instead of filling each with the next item in line. This is an illustration of joint choice, not an additional measured result. The optimality claim applies to the frozen, discretized scheduling problem, not every future event.

results.finding: Task latency fell 26.8%; decode throughput rose 29.5%.
results.setup: DeepSeek-V4 Flash, SWE-Lite, 64 workers, two servers with four H100s each; compared with the best tested baseline per metric, not an average across workloads.

papers.limitations: The trade-off can reverse. On AutomationBench with 128 workers, TAO took longer to produce a first token than Dynamo and trailed ThunderAgent in task latency and throughput. Protecting running sessions can increase the wait before another session starts.
papers.implications: An agent-service operator must decide whether customers value an immediate response, completed jobs, or both. Test the scheduler against that promise using real tool-delay and concurrency traces, then compare infrastructure cost per successful task. Better scheduling could postpone a GPU purchase, but only if completion gains survive peak load without breaking the first-response target. The reported throughput gain alone does not establish that saving.

papers.title: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime
papers.headline: Let the model choose which layer comes next
papers.authors: Abdellah Rahmani, Sean McLeish, Ang Li, Sanae Lotfi, Pascal Frossard, Micah Goldblum
papers.summary: LoL replaces a fixed sequence of Transformer layers with a reusable library. A learned router chooses the next whole layer as computation proceeds.
papers.problem: Conventional Transformers execute layers in a predetermined order. Expert selection and layer skipping add flexibility, but usually preserve that order. LoL asks whether the sequence of computations itself should depend on the input.

method.title: Choose a whole layer, then choose again
method.description: The author implementation builds a shared collection of complete Transformer blocks, with ordinary blocks before and after the routed middle. At each middle step, the router scores the available blocks, selects one per window (a group of tokens), and sends that window to it. The selected block's update is weighted by its routing probability before being added to the current state. Because the next step consults the same collection again, a block can be reused; its position is no longer permanently tied to one depth.

method.title: Make each choice using completed context
method.description: Routing also needs a rule about what it may inspect. The released router computes a summary of earlier windows within the same document and uses that summary to score the next block. It excludes the current window from that history. This gives the choice access to useful context without letting later words influence earlier predictions. The implementation also adds learned noise to routing scores during training, encouraging exploration of alternative blocks, and turns that noise off for evaluation.

method.title: Move the window boundaries to reconnect information
method.description: Separate windows make it possible to send different pieces of text through different blocks, but fixed partitions would restrict which tokens can interact. The attention implementation shifts the partition boundaries as depth increases and processes each resulting window with causal attention. Tokens separated by one boundary can consequently share a later window. The effect is gradual exchange across neighboring groups while preserving the rule that a token can use only preceding context.

results.finding: On GSM8K, LoL scored 27.9%, versus 27.5% for a sliding-window Transformer and 29.7% for a full-attention Transformer.
results.setup: The paper's 1B-parameter, math-trained comparison used approximately 90 ExaFLOPs per run. These results show competitiveness, not a consistent accuracy lead.

papers.limitations: This is an initial architecture study at modest scale. The reported accuracy comparison does not establish lower production latency, and full-attention performance remains higher on GSM8K.
papers.implications: For a model or accelerator team, the near-term decision is how much exploration to fund. Require a matched-quality comparison that includes routing overhead, batching and runtime development effort before assigning a serving-cost advantage to this architecture. A bounded prototype can test whether adaptive execution creates a customer-relevant capability or efficiency gain; committing a product roadmap would require evidence beyond competitive small-model accuracy.

papers.title: CodeQuant2: Enhanced Outlier Mitigation and Adaptive Clustering for Low-Precision LRMs
papers.headline: Low-bit reasoning needs better calibration—and a deployable kernel
papers.authors: Xingyu Liu, Xiangyang Yin, Tianhua Xia, Haiyu Wang, Sai Qian Zhang · NYU
papers.venue: arXiv · v1; author manuscript labeled NeurIPS 2026
papers.summary: CodeQuant2 combines reasoning-aware calibration, learned weight codebooks and lookup-based decoding. Deployment still needs integration.
papers.problem: Reasoning generates long token sequences, making small quantization errors consequential. Calibration on ordinary text can miss early-decoding activation outliers. Meanwhile, decompressing clustered weights before ordinary GEMM introduces memory traffic that can consume the expected inference saving.

method.title: Calibrate where reasoning starts
method.description: The release mixes full-precision GSM8K reasoning prefixes with WikiText-2 at 1:9, using up to 256 generated tokens. It tunes rotation and scaling, allocates codebooks, then tunes centroids and assignments against local reconstruction losses.

method.title: Spend codebook capacity selectively
method.description: Matrices start with 16 centroids. Local reconstruction sensitivity and measured GPU latency guide paired changes to 32 and 8 centroids. Their index widths average four bits across matrices; this is not a claim that every weight uses four bits. Quantization targets Q/K/V and gate/up projections.

method.title: Execute the compressed representation
method.description: The CUDA entrypoint looks up products using packed activation and weight indices, with per-output-channel codebooks and shared-memory tables. Split-K reduction produces outputs without dense weight reconstruction. Callers handle packing; the supplied vLLM evaluation commands do not invoke this kernel.

results.finding: 77.0% average accuracy versus CodeQuant’s 66.4%; BF16 remains at 83.8%.
results.setup: Qwen3-4B-Thinking, A4W4, six math/code benchmarks; AIME uses pass@1. This is a 10.6 percentage-point improvement over CodeQuant, not recovery to full precision.

results.finding: 2.45× decode speedup at batch 1; 2.43× at batch 16.
results.setup: Single NVIDIA A6000, Qwen3-4B-Thinking A4W4 versus BF16; GSM8K-shaped workload with 100 prompt and 4,000 decode tokens. These are decoding measurements, not complete request-cost savings.

papers.limitations: Implementation check, November 11: the kernel supports 16 centroids and 1–16 decoding rows; 8/32-centroid ACA cases need another representation or kernel. Evaluation instead uses reconstructed dense weights and activation fake quantization. Accuracy reproduction does not demonstrate accelerated serving integration.
papers.implications: Editorial assessment: a team serving long reasoning responses should test cost per accepted answer, including retries and generated-token count. Faster decoding helps only if retained quality avoids extra attempts. The commercial opportunity is an integrated quantization-and-serving product: calibration tooling, workload-specific validation and dependable kernels. Before adopting it, budget for connecting the packed representation to the production runtime and measuring concurrency, first-token latency and full-request GPU time. The paper’s speedup alone does not price that integration work.

papers.title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
papers.headline: Better readout from a fixed recurrent memory
papers.authors: Tushaar Gangavarapu, Gil Tabak, Clemens JS Schaefer
papers.summary: Muir shifts gate capacity toward writes and improves how stored context is read.
papers.problem:
Background: linear attention compresses past tokens into a fixed recurrent state. The Gated DeltaNet-2 baseline updates it in three steps: decay old memory, erase the association predicted for the incoming key, then write the new value. Its channel-wise erase and write gates separately control the key and value axes. This makes memory editing more selective than one shared scalar gate.

Muir identifies two costs: expensive full-rank gates and slow-decaying rows dominating readout.

method.title: Allocate capacity by sensitivity
method.description: Normalized keys concentrate energy in fewer channels, making erase updates less sensitive than writes. Lower-rank erase projections free parameters for a wider FFN within the same total budget.

method.title: Rebalance the memory read
method.description: A matched-filter gate reweights the query using static gains and per-token modulation, reducing interference from uneven state-row magnitudes and the need to erase useful associations.

method.title: Fit the training kernel to the hardware
method.description: Boundary-pivoted decay avoids unstable divisions; block matrix products replace sequential triangular solves for large TPU-friendly chunks.

results.finding: Matches GDN-2 training throughput; reaches its validation loss about 1.2× faster.
results.setup: 166M–1.34B models, 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, eight TPU7x chips. Both recurrent models use the new kernel.

papers.limitations: 10M-token perplexity stability is not 10M-token retrieval accuracy. At 1M tokens, static-readout passkey recall is 90.0% zero-shot and 99.4% after a 64K-context cooldown.
papers.implications:
Editorial judgement: this is a useful architecture-and-runtime evaluation candidate for long-session products. Ask whether a fixed state preserves the specific facts that customers need, especially after corrections and several unrelated turns. Average language-model loss alone is a weak acceptance test for that decision.

For an accelerator team, compare matched-quality implementations on the intended device, including prefill, decode and memory usage. The decision should account for kernel porting and model-training effort. A compelling TPU training result can justify an experiment; the product case still needs task accuracy, service latency and the cost of maintaining a separate execution path.

papers.title: MemLLM: End-to-end In-Storage Acceleration of On-device Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Precomputed KV Caches
papers.headline: Move attention to the SSD holding the cache
papers.authors: Seungkwan Kang, Hyungseok Ko, Heemin Kim, Myoungsoo Jung
papers.summary: MemLLM targets on-device RAG where saved prefill compute becomes expensive KV traffic.
papers.problem: Precomputed document KV avoids repeating prefill, but loading it from SSD can leave the GPU waiting on PCIe. Decode-only storage accelerators still leave initial attention on the host. Retrieved documents have new neighbors, so selective recomputation must update context-dependent entries.

method.title: Compute where KV lives
method.description: Per-NAND-channel Elastic-SIMD units process attention; GPU projections and FFNs remain on the host. One datapath handles decode vectors and prefill's thin matrix products; adjacent vector units keep softmax intermediates in registers. Local results combine through online softmax.

method.title: Fuse reads; retain partial results
method.description: Recomputation and new-query attention share one KV pass. A hardware filter substitutes updated entries. Global SRAM reduces partial outputs without controller-DRAM spills.

results.finding: 4.06× average end-to-end speedup
results.setup: Versus GPU-FullCompute: eight RAG datasets, six FP16 models; Jetson Orin NX 16GB with 8GB available. Trace-driven simulation combines profiled GPU kernels, FPGA-derived timing and SimpleSSD.

papers.limitations: Simulated system performance. Additional host memory narrows the reported advantage to 1.83× at 16GB.
papers.implications:
Editorial judgement: an edge-device supplier should first ask whether customers repeatedly query a local document collection large enough to create this transfer problem. Compare a storage accelerator with spending the same product budget on additional DRAM, smaller caches or shorter retrieval context, at matched answer quality and latency.

A convincing product trial should measure the complete user request, including document refresh and cold-cache cases. The purchasing decision also needs SSD cost, endurance, integration effort and software support. Use a prototype to close those gaps before changing a hardware roadmap.
